sections.title: Cost per successful task, not cost per token
sections.body:
Token prices are the number everyone quotes, and the wrong denominator. What a business pays for is **a task done right**. The honest measure is:

> **cost per successful task = (everything spent on all attempts) divided by (the tasks that succeeded)**

'Everything spent' includes more than the model:

| Cost | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| Model tokens | Input, output (usually dearer), and cache reads and writes; reasoning tokens count as output (lesson 15) |
| Tool and retrieval calls | Search, database queries, vector store queries |
| Retries and repeated work | Failed calls retried, loops, duplicate agents in a multi-agent design (lesson 43) |
| Infrastructure | Hosting, queues, storage for traces and checkpoints |
| **People when the agent fails** | Escalations, review time, rework and the cost of an error that gets through |

The last row is the one budgets forget. A failed task is not free: a person takes it over. When we modelled this (next section), the model's own cost was about one percent of the total once those takeovers were counted. That changes what you optimise: **a one-point gain in success rate can be worth far more than a large cut in token price.**

Other levers on the model line, from the vendor's pricing page and guidance: a **smaller model for simpler steps** (Microsoft's guide says classification, extraction and formatting often work on smaller, cheaper models); **prompt caching**, where a cache read costs a tenth of the input price (a twentieth on Opus 5.5) so a long stable prefix such as the system prompt and tool definitions becomes cheap; the **Batch API**, at half price, only for work that can wait; **trimming what enters the context** (lesson 47's trace showed a 96 percent cut in input tokens from returning three log lines instead of the whole log); and **fewer steps**. Watch one trap the page names: Claude 4.7 and later models use a newer tokenizer that produces about 30 percent more tokens for the same text, so a comparison of two models by price per token alone mis-states their cost for the same task.
sections.example: Fictional. A task costs $0.013 in model tokens and succeeds 92.5 percent of the time. Of 10,000 tasks, 750 fail and each failure costs $15 of a person's time. The model bill is about $130 a day; the failure bill is about $11,250 a day. The first number is what the invoice shows; the second is what the project really costs.
sections.common_mistake: Comparing two designs on cost per call or per million tokens. Compare cost per successful task including the cost of the failures.
sections.check_question: Why is cost per successful task a better measure than cost per token, and what is the cost most budgets forget?
sections.check_answer: A cheap run that fails still costs something and leaves the task undone, so the cost of the failures belongs in the figure. The forgotten cost is people taking over failed tasks (escalation, review and rework).

sections.title: A model of two designs at 10,000 tasks a day
sections.body:
The criterion asks you to compute cost per successful task and median latency for two model-tier designs at 10,000 tasks a day, with assumptions and an uncertainty range, and to pick one. Here is our worked version for the DataOps agent. The two designs:

- **Design A:** Claude Sonnet 5.5 for every model step ($2 input, $10 output per million tokens).
- **Design B:** Claude Haiku 4.5 for the read-only diagnoses (tier 2; $1 input, $5 output) and Sonnet 5.5 only for tier-3 diagnose-and-propose.

The assumptions (all ours except the prices, the 0.1 cache-read factor and the 30 percent tokenizer figure): 30 percent of tasks reach tier 3 (range 20 to 40); the system prompt and tool definitions (1,800 tokens) are read from the cache; a task takes 3 model calls (4 at tier 3); the log is about 600 tokens (range 300 to 1,200); 2 to 15 percent of calls are retried; Sonnet succeeds on 93 percent of tasks (range 88 to 97), Haiku on 85 percent of tier-2 tasks (range 75 to 92); a person takes over each failure at $15 (range $8 to $30). Each uncertain input is drawn from a triangular distribution over its range, over 60 simulated days of 10,000 tasks, so the output has a spread. The code is `cost.py`.

Results (10th, 50th and 90th percentiles across days):

| | Design A (Sonnet for all) | Design B (Haiku tier 2, Sonnet tier 3) |
|---|---|---|
| Success rate | 92.5 percent | 86.5 percent |
| Model cost per day | $106 / $121 / $142 | $68 / $78 / $89 |
| Model cost per successful task | $0.0117 / $0.0130 / $0.0156 | $0.0079 / $0.0090 / $0.0101 |
| **Total per successful task, including people taking over failures** | **$0.93 / $1.35 / $1.98** | **$1.92 / $2.61 / $3.99** |
| Median task latency (assumed formula) | 9.4 / 9.6 / 9.9 s | 5.2 / 5.3 / 5.4 s |

Read it carefully:

1. **B is cheaper on the model bill** by about $43 a day at the median (a third), and faster by about 4 seconds, **but twice as expensive overall**, because its assumed lower success rate sends about 600 more tasks a day to people. Each point of success on the 7,000 tier-2 tasks is 70 tasks, worth about $1,050 a day, against a saving of $43 a day in tokens.
2. **The break-even is stark:** at the most likely inputs, B matches A on total cost only if Haiku succeeds on 93.0 percent of tier-2 tasks, which is Sonnet's own rate. The saving never pays for a worse success rate.
3. **So the decision rests on a number we assumed,** Haiku's success rate. If you *measure* that Haiku matches Sonnet on your tier-2 cases, B wins on cost and speed. If it is a few points lower, A wins. That is why the evaluation (lesson 46) is a finance tool as well as a quality tool. And it needs enough cases to see the difference: to tell 85 from 93 percent you need far more than 25 (lesson 18 gave about 120 per version to separate 70 from 85).

**Pick one:** on these assumptions, choose **A**, and run the measurement that would change the answer (a tier-2 evaluation on both models, with at least a hundred cases) before adopting B. Record the decision with the date of the prices and the assumptions, so it can be revisited.
sections.example:
```text
Design A: success 92.5%
   model cost per day (10/50/90th)            $106 / 121 / 142
   incl. people taking over failures, per success $0.926 / 1.353 / 1.978
   median task latency, seconds                9.4 / 9.6 / 9.9
Design B: success 86.5%
   model cost per day (10/50/90th)            $68 / 78 / 89
   incl. people taking over failures, per success $1.915 / 2.614 / 3.993
   median task latency, seconds                5.2 / 5.3 / 5.4

Break-even at the most likely inputs: Design B matches Design A on total cost per success ($1.141) only if Haiku succeeds on 93.0% of tier-2 tasks (Sonnet: 93%).
```
sections.common_mistake: Presenting the median as 'the cost'. Give the range, say what drives it (here success rate and the cost of a takeover), and say which assumptions you would measure first.
sections.check_question: In our model Design B is cheaper on tokens but dearer overall. Why, and what single measurement would change the decision?
sections.check_answer: Its assumed lower success rate sends many more tasks to people, and each takeover costs far more than the token saving. Measuring Haiku's success rate on your tier-2 cases: if it matches Sonnet's, B wins.

sections.title: Latency, caching and routing, and how to report it
sections.body:
**Latency** matters as much as cost for a product. For an agent, task latency is the sum of its steps (each model call, each tool call, any wait for a person). Three points:

- **Report percentiles, not an average.** A median of 9 seconds with a 95th percentile of 40 is a different product from one that is always 9. Our model reports the median per day with its spread; real traces (lesson 47) give you the actual distribution.
- **Where time goes:** in our model most of it is model calls; their time grows with input size (a bigger prompt reads slower) and output length. Smaller models are faster. Cutting a tool's output (lesson 47) cut both tokens and time.
- **Interactive versus background:** a person waiting needs seconds; an overnight diagnosis can wait, and can use cheaper, slower options such as the Batch API (half price, but not interactive and not available with some features).

**Routing** is deciding which model handles which step. A cheap router that sends easy cases to a small model and hard ones to a larger one can pay off, but the router itself can be wrong, and a wrong route costs a failure. Our Design B is a static route (by tier). Evaluate any routing the way lesson 44 evaluates handoffs: measure the confusion, not only the average.

**Caching** is the cheapest saving when a long prefix repeats: with a cache read at one tenth of the input price (the pricing page, 2026-10-02), a 1,800-token prefix read from the cache costs about as much as 180 fresh tokens. It only helps if the prefix is identical and the cache stays warm; a volume of 10,000 tasks a day keeps it warm, a handful a day may not. Put stable content (system prompt, tool definitions) first and variable content last.

**What to report to a stakeholder.** One table: cost per successful task (range) including people, median and p95 latency, the success rate and how it was measured (cases, trials), the two or three assumptions the answer is most sensitive to, the date of each price, and the measurement you would run next. That is also the content of the one-page business case in Module 12.
sections.example: Fictional sentence for a steering committee: 'At 10,000 tasks a day the agent costs about $1.35 per successfully handled task including staff takeovers (range $0.93 to $1.98), against $X today. The result is most sensitive to success rate and takeover cost; we will measure success on 100 more tier-2 cases before choosing the cheaper model.'
sections.common_mistake: Quoting latency from a single demo run. Production latency has a distribution, includes waiting and retries, and depends on load.
sections.check_question: Give two ways to lower the cost of an agent run without lowering its success rate, one on tokens and one on routing.
sections.check_answer: Tokens: cache the stable prefix (cache reads cost a tenth) or trim what enters the context. Routing: send simple steps to a smaller model, but only after measuring that its success rate on those steps matches.

sections.title: Do it: lab
sections.body:
1. Take your DataOps agent. Write down its flow and the tokens per step from a real trace (lesson 47). Write each assumption you will make for volume, tier mix, success rate and cost of a failure, with a low, likely and high value.
2. Compute, with code, cost per successful task and median latency for two model-tier designs at 10,000 tasks a day. Use current prices from the vendor's page and record the date. Include the cost of failures taken over by people.
3. Report each as a range (10th, 50th, 90th percentile) from a simulation over your assumption ranges, not a single number.
4. Find the break-even: what success rate for the cheaper design makes it match the dearer one? State what measurement would tell you which side you are on, and how many cases it needs.
5. Pick one design and write the decision in five lines: the choice, the assumptions it depends on most, the measurement you will run next, the date of the prices and when you will revisit.

**Done when:** you have cost per successful task (with people costs) and median latency for two designs as ranges at 10,000 tasks a day, a break-even success rate, a chosen design, and a note of the assumptions and the measurement that would change the choice, with the price date.

sections.title: Interview check
sections.body: Answer aloud first, then compare. Do not memorise the words; understand the shape.
sections.check_question: How would you estimate the cost of running an AI agent at scale?
sections.check_answer:
1. Cost per successful task, not per token: all spend on all attempts divided by successes, including retries, tools, infrastructure and the people who take over failures.
2. A model of the flow from real traces: tokens per step, tier mix, retries, with ranges for every uncertain input, simulated to give a range rather than one number.
3. Compare designs on that figure and on median and p95 latency; check break-evens, since a cheaper model only wins if its success rate holds.
4. Levers: smaller models for simple steps, prompt caching of the stable prefix, trimming context, batch for background work, fewer steps.
5. State which assumptions the answer is most sensitive to, date the prices, and measure the key one (usually success rate on a representative set) before committing.

sections.title: Evidence to keep
sections.body: Keep the model code, the assumption table with ranges, the results table, the break-even, the decision note and the price date. They feed the business case in Module 12.
